answer.label: Not Lao Tzu’s words — a modern paraphrase
answer.authorDates: fl. 6th century BCE (traditional) · semi-legendary Chinese sage, reputed author of the Tao Te Ching
answer.sourceLine: The idea is authentically Daoist, but this exact English sentence is a modern paraphrase — it appears in no standard translation of the Tao Te Ching. It condenses the wu wei teaching of chapter 37, whose actual line reads “The way never acts, yet nothing is left undone” — the words “nature,” “hurry” and “accomplished” are not in any recognized rendering.

source.heading: Where the idea really comes from

docMeta.dd: “The way never acts, yet nothing is left undone”
Modern paraphrase — no known translator or source

source.excerpt: “The way never acts, yet nothing is left undone.” — Tao Te Ching, ch. 37 (trans. D. C. Lau). The Chinese — 道常無為，而無不為 — literally reads “the Way is constantly non-acting, yet there is nothing it does not do.” Nowhere does it mention “nature,” “hurry,” or things being “accomplished.”
trail: The exact sentence is credited to Lao Tzu across quote sites but with no work, chapter, or translator — Goodreads lists it with 1,400+ likes and no source ↗.

A compilation of many published translations of Tao Te Ching chapter 37 ↗ shows renderings such as Legge’s “there is nothing which it does not do” and Le Guin’s “the Way never does anything, and everything gets done” — none uses “nature does not hurry.”
The line does not appear among the sourced or even the disputed/misattributed quotations on Wikiquote’s Laozi page ↗, consistent with it being an unsourced modern coinage.
source.excerptNote: The popular one-liner fuses this chapter’s “nothing left undone” with a general “unhurried” feel, but matches no published rendering word-for-word.

That wording is an anonymous modern paraphrase with no identifiable translator and no evidence of pre-1931 publication, so we assert no copyright status. (Standard scholarly translations of chapter 37 — e.g. D. C. Lau, 1963; Gia-Fu Feng, 1972 — remain under their own copyrights, but this sentence is not from any of them.)

author.bio: Lao Tzu (“Old Master,” also romanized Laozi) is the semi-legendary figure traditionally credited with founding philosophical Daoism and composing the Tao Te Ching. Modern scholars regard him as quasi-mythical and the text as a layered compilation reaching its familiar form around the 4th–3rd centuries BCE. The book’s central teaching of wu wei — effortless, non-forcing action in harmony with the Way — is the genuine source of the sentiment behind this popular quote.

misattribution.heading: A real idea, an invented sentence
misattribution.intro: This is the classic “ancient wisdom” paraphrase: the sentiment is genuinely Daoist, but the polished English one-liner is modern and traceable to no translator.

items.why: “Nature does not hurry, yet everything is accomplished” appears in no standard translation of the Tao Te Ching. A survey of many published versions of chapter 37 ↗ turns up nothing using “nature,” “hurry,” or “accomplished” — the authentic line is “the way never acts, yet nothing is left undone.”

The concept — effortless, non-forcing action (wu wei) that nonetheless leaves nothing undone — is authentically Lao Tzu’s, so crediting the sentiment to him is fair even though the sentence is not his words.

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: the thought is Lao Tzu’s (Tao Te Ching ch. 37 ↗), but the exact sentence is an unsourced modern paraphrase — not a real translation.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The quote endures because it captures a real and central Daoist intuition: that the natural world produces abundant results without strain, striving, or haste. In the Tao Te Ching, this is the doctrine of wu wei — often translated “non-action” or “effortless action” — the idea that the most effective way to act is to stop forcing and move with the grain of things.

What makes the modern sentence so shareable is exactly what makes it inauthentic: it is smoother, more aphoristic, and more “productivity”-friendly than any literal rendering. The scholarly line — “the way never acts, yet nothing is left undone” — is more paradoxical and less reassuring than the polished English motto that circulates on wellness and calm-app graphics.
detailsBody: Chapter 37 opens the second (“Te”) half of the received text in some arrangements and states the wu wei principle at cosmic scale: the Way does nothing deliberate, yet nothing is left undone. Related unhurried imagery appears elsewhere (e.g. chapter 73’s description of Heaven’s Way as at ease yet effective), which is likely why the paraphrase blends “does not hurry” with chapter 37’s “nothing left undone.”
context.pull: The idea is Lao Tzu’s. The sentence is ours — a modern age’s.
